# The cognitive process model

The task model says what a participant is asked to do. The cognitive process model
says what doing it is thought to engage. It is a list of standard mental processes,
each hypothesized to be associated with one or more tasks, and the links between the
processes and the tasks. This page describes the model as it stands; the rules behind
it are the [process criteria](methods/process_criteria/index.md).

## What a cognitive process is

A **cognitive process** is a mental operation hypothesized to occur in a participant
during a trial, such as response inhibition, working memory updating or reward
anticipation. A candidate qualifies when three questions can plausibly be answered
about it:

1. **When does it happen?** At what point in a trial, relative to stimulus and
   response, is it engaged?
2. **How is it elicited?** What stimulus structure, instruction or contingency drives
   it?
3. **How is it measured?** What behavioral, physiological or neural signature indexes
   it, even imperfectly?

Things of another kind are left out: states and traits, specific emotions, stimulus
categories, individual-difference constructs, task parameters, analysis methods, and
umbrella terms such as "attention" or "memory". The
[process selection criteria](methods/process_criteria/01_process_selection_criteria.md)
give the full rule.

There are {{ n_processes }} processes. Each has an identifier of the form
`hed_<slug>`, a name, aliases where the literature uses more than one name, a
definition, references, and the list of tasks linked to it.

## Categories

The processes are grouped into {{ n_categories }} **categories**, such as inhibitory
control and conflict monitoring, long-term memory, and reward anticipation and
motivation. A category groups processes by research tradition for browsing and carries
a scope statement. Categories are labels, not a hierarchy: a category is not a
process, and a process inherits nothing from its category. The umbrella terms excluded
as processes survive here, as the names of categories. See
[Cognitive processes](processes/index.md) for the list.

## Links between tasks and processes

A task is **linked** to a process when the task is designed to engage it. A link is
justified when at least one of three things holds:

- the papers that define the task theorize that it engages the process (Stroop and
  interference control);
- a standard contrast between conditions of the task is interpreted as isolating the
  process (congruent against incongruent trials and conflict monitoring);
- a standard measure of the task is interpreted as an index of the process (the
  stop-signal reaction time and response inhibition).

A link is a hypothesis taken from the literature. It is not a measurement, not an
ontology assertion, and not a claim that the task engages nothing else; it records
what the task is designed to probe. The
[task linkage rules](methods/process_criteria/06_task_linkage_rules.md) give the detail.

There are {{ n_links }} links. Each task in the catalog is linked to at least one
process, and {{ n_linked }} of the {{ n_processes }} processes are linked to at least
one task; the rest are kept because a task that engages them may be added. A variant
of a task can add processes to those of its standard form. The
[task-process links](task_process_links.md) page lists every link in both directions.

## How the two models fit together

The two models are kept separate on purpose. The task model is built from what can be
read in a methods section: what was shown, what was asked, what was at stake. It does
not depend on any theory of what the task measures, so two people with different
theories can agree on it. The process model carries the theory, as explicit links that
can be questioned one at a time.

Together they allow two kinds of comparison:

- **By what the participant does.** Tasks with the same game type and rules are
  compared part by part, whatever processes they are said to engage.
- **By what the task is thought to engage.** Tasks that are different games but are
  linked to the same process can be grouped for a question about that process.

They also allow a check that neither gives alone: when tasks that are the same game
are linked to different processes, or very different games to the same process, the
links are worth a second look.

The cognitive process model has not yet been revised in the way the task model has.
Its processes and links are those established for the task catalog, and they are
expected to be reviewed as the tasks of papers and datasets are modeled.
